```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

# --- CONFIGURATION ---
# Set the name of the target distribution matching your simulation[cite: 2]
TARGET_DIST <- "cauchy" 

# Adjust output directory path to match where your files were written[cite: 2]
data_dir <- "~/SJSU26F/MATH167R/CLT/data/cauchy"

# Load saved simulation dataset and add necessary columns for tables[cite: 2]
summary_table <- read.csv(file.path(data_dir, "cauchy_metrics.csv")) %>%
  mutate(
    mean_bias = sim_mean - theo_mean,
    se_ratio = sim_se / theo_se
  )
```

## 1. Original Population Distribution

<!-- Question 1: What does the original population distribution look like? -->

- **Name / Class:** `r TARGET_DIST`
- **Type:** Continuous, symmetric, extremely heavy-tailed\[cite: 2\]
- **Description:**
  <!-- Describe features: continuity, boundedness, symmetry/skewness, support, unimodal vs multimodal, etc. -->
  The Cauchy distribution is a continuous, symmetrical distribution with
  very heavy tails. This distribution is helpful in physics and
  financial returns where outliers are more present than standard
  distributions.

```{r}
#| label: fig-population-shape
#| fig-cap: "Theoretical / baseline shape of the population distribution (n = 1)."

ggplot() +
  xlim(-10, 10) +
  stat_function(fun = dcauchy, args = list(location=0, scale=1), color = "#E69F00", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = paste("Population Density:", TARGET_DIST),
    x = "x",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2. Theoretical Mean and Standard Deviation

- **Theoretical Mean (**$\mu$): Undefined (NA)\[cite: 2\]
- **Theoretical Standard Deviation (**$\sigma$): Undefined (NA)\[cite:
  2\]

For a standard Cauchy distribution, the PDF is:

$$f(x) = \frac{1}{\pi(1 + x^2)}$$

The theoretical mean is undefined because the integral does not
absolutely converge:

$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x \frac{1}{\pi(1 + x^2)} \, dx \to \text{Undefined}$$

Since the mean is undefined, the variance and theoretical standard
deviation are also undefined, representing an infinitely heavy tail.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 3. Rate of Convergence to Normality

<!-- Question 3: How quickly does the sampling distribution become approximately normal? -->

- **Observations across sample sizes (**$n$):
  <!-- At what sample size n does skewness drop close to 0? Kurtosis near 0? -->
  This distribution is symmetrical which means while simulation can add
  some fluctuation, it will have a low amount of skewness. The excess
  kurtosis levels are extremely high

```{r}
#| label: fig-shape-statistics
#| fig-cap: "Convergence of Skewness and Excess Kurtosis toward zero as sample size increases."

summary_table %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(skewness, excess_kurtosis), names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = value, color = metric)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("skewness" = "#E69F00", "excess_kurtosis" = "#E69F00")) +
  labs(
    title = paste("Shape Statistics vs. n for", TARGET_DIST),
    x = "Sample Size (n)",
    y = "Metric Value",
    color = "Metric"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

::: callout-note
### Important to note

<!-- Add note about specific behavior for this distribution here -->As
the sample mean size increases, excess kurtosis grows!
:::

## 4. Simulated Mean vs. Theoretical Mean

<!-- Question 4: How does the simulated mean compare with the theoretical mean? -->

```{r}
#| label: tbl-mean-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Comparison of simulated sample means vs. theoretical mean."

summary_table %>%
  select(n, theo_mean, sim_mean, mean_bias) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("n", "Theoretical Mean (μ)", "Simulated Mean (X̄)", "Mean Bias (X̄ - μ)")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"))
```

- **Analysis:**
  <!-- Does the empirical mean stay close to the theoretical mean across all n? Is there any noticeable bias? -->
  We cannot calculate this because the theoretical mean does not exist.

## 5. Simulated Standard Error vs. Theoretical Standard Error

<!-- Question 5: How does the simulated standard error compare with SE(X̄) = σ / √n? -->

$$\text{SE}(\bar{X}) = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$$

```{r}
#| label: tbl-se-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Comparison of simulated standard errors with theoretical SE = σ / √n."

summary_table %>%
  select(n, theo_se, sim_se, se_ratio) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("n", "Theoretical SE", "Simulated SE", "SE Ratio (Sim / Theo)")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"))
```

- **Analysis:**
  <!-- Does the ratio sim_se / theo_se remain close to 1.0? Does the empirical spread decay at rate 1 / √n? -->
  We cannot calculate this because the theoretical standard error does
  not exist.

## 6. Evidence for Normality

<!-- Question 6: What evidence supports your conclusion that the distribution is—or is not—approximately normal? -->

### Graphical Evidence (Density & Q-Q Plots)

```{r}
#| label: fig-normal-dist-qq
#| fig-cap: "Standardized empirical density and Normal Q-Q plots across selected sample sizes $n$ ($B = 10{,}000$)."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-align: "center"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(patchwork)

set.seed(8676)

B <- 10000L
selected_n <- c(1, 10, 30, 100)

density_qq_list <- list()

for (n_val in selected_n) {
  observations <- rcauchy(B * n_val, location = 0, scale = 1)
  sample_matrix <- matrix(observations, nrow = B, ncol = n_val)
  means <- rowMeans(sample_matrix)
  
  sim_mean <- mean(means)
  sim_se <- sd(means)
  
  z_means <- if (is.finite(sim_se) && sim_se > 0) (means - sim_mean) / sim_se else rep(NA_real_, B)
  density_qq_list[[length(density_qq_list) + 1]] <- data.frame(
    n_label = paste0("n = ", n_val),
    n_num = n_val,
    z = z_means
  )
}

plot_data <- bind_rows(density_qq_list) %>% filter(is.finite(z))
plot_data$n_label <- factor(plot_data$n_label, levels = paste0("n = ", selected_n))

tight_theme <- theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold"),
    plot.margin = margin(t = 4, r = 6, b = 4, l = 6)
  )

p_dens_tight <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = z)) +
  geom_density(fill = "#E69F00", alpha = 0.35, color = "#E69F00", linewidth = 0.6) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = 0, sd = 1), linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +
  facet_wrap(~ n_label, nrow = 2, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Empirical Density vs N(0,1)", x = "Standardized Mean (Z)", y = "Density") +
  tight_theme

p_qq_tight <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(sample = z)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray30") +
  stat_qq(color = "#E69F00", alpha = 0.15, size = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ n_label, nrow = 2) +
  labs(title = "Normal Q-Q Plots", x = "Theoretical Quantiles", y = "Sample Quantiles") +
  tight_theme

p_dens_tight | p_qq_tight
```

- **Density Overlays:**
  <!-- Mention the alignment with the standard N(0, 1) curve. -->The
  density overlay is no where near the standard normal distribution.
- **Q-Q Plot Quantile Alignment:**
  <!-- Inspect the linearity in your Q-Q plots. -->The Q-Q plot while
  linear does not align with standard normal Q-Q plot values.

### Statistical Evidence (Shapiro-Wilk Test & Moment Ratios)

```{r}
#| label: tbl-normality-metrics
#| tbl-cap: "Normality assessment metrics: Skewness, Kurtosis, and Shapiro-Wilk test."

summary_table %>%
  select(n, skewness, excess_kurtosis, shapiro_W, shapiro_p) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("n", "Skewness", "Excess Kurtosis", "Shapiro-Wilk W", "p-value")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"))
```

- **Conclusion on Normality:**
  <!-- Summarize when the distribution meets practical and formal normality thresholds. -->
  The skewness values and excess kurtosis are extremely variable due to
  the outlier producing nature of this distribution. The Shapiro-Wilk W
  value never even comes close to 1.0.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 7. Limitations and Surprises

<!-- Question 7: What limitations or surprises did you observe? -->

- **Key Observations / Surprises:**
  <!-- e.g., persistent tail skewness, boundary effects, Shapiro-Wilk p-value sensitivity to large sample sizes, etc. -->There
  is no skewness but the heavy tailed nature of the Cauchy distribution
  makes it impossible to converge. Even though it is a common
  distribution it does not appear to follow the typical rules of other
  distributions. I am surprised that it never converges, and actually
  the excess kurtosis grows rapidly as sample sizes get larger. It
  clearly does not adhere to the Central Limit Theorem.
- **Simulation Limitations:**
  <!-- e.g., finite Monte Carlo reps B = 10,000, fixed selection of n_values, truncation of sub-sample size for normality testing. -->Monte
  Carlo simulation has a large effect on this distribution as seen in
  the skewness which does not converge. It appears that the skewness
  converges at first glance but the values are so high that it does not.
  Other distributions converge to zero meaning there is extremely small
  chance that some extremely high outlier occur but that is not the case
  with the Cauchy.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 8. Final Verdict

#### Central Limit Theorem *Does Not Apply*

<!-- Final thoughts on convergence -->The Central Limit Theorem does not
apply to this distribution. There were some warning signs based on the
inability to calculate theoretical standard error and mean. In practice
the possibility of outliers presents itself very strongly and makes
convergence impossible. There is no smoothing that occurs because the
heavy tails will always win and skew the model.
